issues.item: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For a toxic chemical exposure trauma, a weapons-related visual trigger is hard to reconcile clinically unless there is evidence of a separate assault or combat-related trauma. The other trigger items (loss of autonomy, being watched) could occur in medical, workplace, or contamination-related contexts, but weapons specifically points to a qualitatively different trauma context and is therefore not coherent with the stated trauma type.

vignette: Linh had always taken pride in her work as a tattoo artist. She loved the precision and creativity it required, and her clients adored her attention to detail. But that all changed one fateful day when she was accidentally exposed to toxic chemicals at the shop where she worked. The incident left her feeling shaken and vulnerable, like her body had been invaded. As time passed, Linh began to notice that certain smells triggered a wave of anxiety in her. Hospital or antiseptic scents would transport her back to the moment of exposure, making her feel lightheaded and disoriented. She found herself avoiding hospitals, clinics, and even some medical-themed tattoos that clients requested. It wasn't just the smell itself, but what it represented - a loss of control over her own body. At work, Linh started to feel like she was being watched all the time. She would catch glimpses of people staring at her out of the corner of her eye, or sense that someone was lurking nearby. This feeling of constant surveillance made her skin crawl, and she began to wonder if anyone was monitoring her health after the exposure. Her mind would wander to worst-case scenarios - cancer, organ damage, permanent disability. The paranoia spilled over into her personal life as well. Linh's husband, Tuan, noticed that she had become increasingly withdrawn and isolated. She would hesitate to make decisions or take charge of everyday tasks, fearing that someone else might be controlling the outcome. "I just feel like I'm not in control anymore," she confessed to him one day. "Like my body is a ticking time bomb." As the months went by, Linh's behavior became more erratic. She would turn down tattoo commissions if they involved working with certain chemicals or dyes. Her relationships with clients began to suffer, and her reputation as an artist started to slip. Tuan encouraged her to seek help, but Linh was resistant - she didn't want to admit that the exposure had changed her so profoundly. It wasn't until a particularly grueling tattoo session left her in tears that Linh realized she needed support. She couldn't shake off the feeling of being watched or the constant fear of losing autonomy over her body. With Tuan's prodding, Linh finally agreed to see a therapist, hoping to break free from the suffocating grip of anxiety and reclaim control over her life. As she sat in the waiting room, Linh couldn't help but notice the hospital smell wafting through the air. It made her stomach turn, but this time, instead of fleeing, she took a deep breath and steeled herself for what was to come. Maybe, just maybe, this was the first step towards reclaiming her autonomy - and her art.
